question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. The SNP heritability represents the total variance in a phenotype that can be attributed to all measured SNPs in the population, but a polygenic score is derived from effect-size estimates in a finite discovery sample. This introduces statistical noise, incomplete linkage disequilibrium tagging, winner’s-curse inflation of effect sizes, and population-specific allele-frequency differences, all of which reduce the out-of-sample R² below the SNP-heritability ceiling. Even with very large samples these practical limitations persist, so the predictive ability of any realizable polygenic score must be strictly lower than the SNP heritability.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance that would be explained if every SNP’s true additive effect were known exactly. A polygenic score (PGS), however, is constructed from estimated effect sizes obtained in a finite discovery sample. Because those estimates contain sampling error, shrinkage, incomplete tagging, and possible mismatch between discovery and target populations, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by any PGS is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Equality is attained only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained samples; for any real PGS the inequality therefore holds. Hence the statement is true.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by all SNPs in aggregate, which is an upper bound derived from the full set of genetic variants. A polygenic score, by contrast, is built from a finite discovery sample and therefore relies on estimated effect sizes that are subject to sampling error, winner's curse, and imperfect tagging of causal variants. Even in the best-case scenario with large but finite samples, these estimation inaccuracies mean that the out-of-sample variance captured by the score must fall short of the SNP-heritability ceiling; only if every causal effect were known without error (an unattainable condition in practice) could the two quantities be equal. Hence the predictive ability measured by R² is necessarily lower.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. The SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance tagged by all SNPs in the population (i.e., the upper bound under an additive model). A polygenic score, however, is constructed from a finite discovery sample in which effect-size estimates are subject to sampling error, winner’s-curse inflation, and imperfect tagging; consequently the out-of-sample variance explained by the resulting score is a downward-biased estimator of that SNP-heritability ceiling. Even with optimal shrinkage methods the realized R² cannot reach the population parameter because the estimation noise is never entirely eliminated.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by all SNPs together in the population. A polygenic score, however, is a finite linear combination of estimated SNP effects derived from a finite discovery sample. Because those effect-size estimates contain sampling error and because not every causal variant is perfectly tagged or included, the out-of-sample R² achieved by the score is bounded above by the SNP heritability and, in practice, is strictly lower. This gap is a direct consequence of the estimation process itself rather than merely a limitation of sample size; even with perfect tagging, the shrinkage or regularization required to produce stable weights prevents the score from recovering the full SNP heritability. Therefore the statement is true.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

SNP heritability (\(h^2_{SNP}\)) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the optimal linear predictor constructed from all measured SNPs. A polygenic score is precisely such a linear predictor; therefore, with infinite training-sample size and perfect effect-size estimates, its out-of-sample \(R^2\) can asymptotically equal (but not exceed) \(h^2_{SNP}\). In finite samples the observed \(R^2\) is lower, yet the statement claims the inequality is *necessarily* strict—an assertion that does not hold in the theoretical limit. Hence the claim is false.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

A polygenic score, by contrast, is constructed from estimated effect sizes obtained from a finite GWAS. Because those estimates contain sampling error, the correlation between the estimated and true scores is necessarily less than 1; consequently the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by the PGS is strictly smaller than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Equality is attained only in the theoretical limit of infinite discovery-sample size, which is never realized in practice. Hence the statement is true.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the SNPs in a multiple regression (i.e., the population \(R^2\) obtained when every SNP is entered simultaneously with its true coefficient). A polygenic score is simply one particular linear combination of those same SNPs. When the weights equal the true population coefficients, the PGS therefore attains exactly \(h^2_{SNP}\). Hence the predictive \(R^2\) of a PGS is bounded above by, but not necessarily strictly below, SNP heritability. In finite samples the realized PGS \(R^2\) will usually fall short because the weights must be estimated, yet the logical upper bound itself is \(h^2_{SNP}\), so the claim that it is “necessarily lower” is false.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. The SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be attributed to the additive effects of all measured SNPs in the population. In contrast, a polygenic score is constructed from a finite discovery sample whose effect-size estimates contain sampling error and winner’s-curse bias; these imperfections necessarily attenuate the out-of-sample R² relative to the SNP-heritability ceiling. Even with optimal weighting and no population stratification, the measurement error in the estimated coefficients guarantees that the variance explained by the score will be strictly lower.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability of a phenotype represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is tagged by (and thus in principle predictable from) the additive effects of all measured SNPs. This quantity is an upper bound on the out-of-sample R² that any linear predictor constructed from those SNPs can achieve. A polygenic score is one such predictor, but its weights are estimated from finite data and are therefore subject to sampling error, shrinkage, imperfect LD tagging, and possible model misspecification. Consequently its predictive R² cannot exceed—and in all realistic settings is strictly lower than—the SNP heritability. Only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained samples would the two quantities converge; under any practical conditions the inequality is strict.

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP-based heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the best linear predictor that uses all measured SNPs. A polygenic score is simply one (finite-sample) estimator of that same predictor. In the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained samples and known causal effects, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) of the polygenic score therefore converges to \(h^2_{SNP}\). Hence the predictive \(R^2\) is bounded above by SNP heritability but is not necessarily strictly lower. 

(The practical gap that is almost always observed arises from estimation error, imperfect LD, winner’s curse, etc., but these are contingent limitations, not definitional necessities.)
